questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics is rolling out one shared Claude Project for its dispatch planners. Six planners work in shifts, and the Project is used for handovers, rate checks and carrier queries.
questions.stem: The Project has been created and the dispatch manual, the driver-hours rules and three months of shift handovers were added as knowledge. Nobody has written any instructions. Planners now get anything from a two-line reply to a page of tables, depending on who asked and when. What is the MOST useful next step?

options.text: Ask each planner to add their own preferred answer length to the Project instructions.
Add Project instructions that state the Project's purpose, who it answers for, the tone to use, and the format each type of answer should take.
Summarise the three months of handovers into one file and replace the originals with it.
Switch the Project to the most capable model, since consistency is mainly a capability problem.

questions.explanation: Project knowledge is reference material — the facts Claude draws on. **Instructions** are what tell it how to behave, and they apply to every chat in the Project, which is exactly what is needed to stop the shape of the answer depending on who asked. Naming the purpose, the audience, the tone and the expected format turns one Project into a consistent service instead of six different assistants.

whyWrong.A: Six people editing shared instructions recreates the conflicting-edit problem, and personal length preferences belong in each person's own settings rather than in shared configuration.
whyWrong.C: Summarising handovers discards detail Claude may legitimately need, and it does nothing about the format varying between chats.
whyWrong.D: Consistency of shape comes from configuration. A more capable model will follow whatever instructions it is given — here, none.

questions.mindset: Knowledge is what Claude reads; instructions are how it should answer, in every chat of the Project.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics' dispatch Project relies on an approved price list that lives in the company's shared drive.
questions.stem: The Project's instructions say: "Always price jobs from Pricing_Q3.xlsx." The logistics team renamed that file last week to `Pricing_2026_Q3.xlsx`. Since then Claude says it cannot find pricing information and has started falling back to general market rates, well above the company's. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Update the instruction to name the new filename, and add a note asking the team to tell the Project owner before renaming anything.
Reword the instruction to refer to the team's current approved pricing document in the Project's knowledge, keeping the rule that prices come only from there.
Paste the current price list into the top of the Project instructions so the figures are always visible to Claude.
Add a fallback line telling Claude to use a sensible market rate if it cannot find the named pricing file.

questions.explanation: Referring to knowledge **by filename** couples a standing rule to a name that will change again. Describing the source by what it is — the current approved pricing document held in the Project's knowledge — survives renames, re-exports and version bumps. Keeping the "only from there" part matters as much as the reference: without it, Claude is licensed to fill the gap.

whyWrong.A: This keeps the fragility and just swaps in a different filename. The next rename breaks it again, and a process note does not fix it.
whyWrong.C: This copies the fact into the instructions, creating a second place to update every quarter — and pricing that disagrees between instructions and knowledge is worse than either alone.
whyWrong.D: Authorising a guess is exactly the behaviour that produced over-priced quotes. The fallback should be to say the price is unavailable, not to invent one.

questions.mindset: Write instructions against the content of your knowledge, never against a filename that can change.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Legal runs eleven shared Claude Projects for its paralegal and fee-earner teams: clause drafting, matter intake, billing queries, witness statements and so on.
questions.stem: Colleagues routinely open the wrong Project, or open the right one and then ask for things it was never set up to do. A paralegal on the intake team wants to change the configuration to fix this. Which TWO changes address it? Choose TWO.

options.text: Write each Project's description to state its purpose, who it is for, what sources it draws on and who maintains it.
Add a line to every Project's instructions telling Claude to suggest a better-suited Project when it is asked something out of scope.
Rename each Project so its name lists every topic and document type it covers.
Merge the eleven Projects into one Project holding all the knowledge, with detailed instructions for each use case.

questions.explanation: Two different problems need two different layers. **Choosing** the right Project happens before anyone types, so it is solved by the **description**, which is written for humans and states purpose, audience, sources and owner. **Staying inside scope** is a behaviour, so it belongs in the **instructions**, with a redirect rather than a refusal so the colleague is helped rather than blocked.

whyWrong.C: A name can only carry a couple of words. Cramming every topic and document type into eleven names produces unreadable labels that help nobody choose.
whyWrong.D: Merging destroys the scoping that makes each Project reliable: every chat would see instructions and knowledge for eleven unrelated workflows, and curation becomes impossible.

questions.mindset: The description is for humans choosing a Project; the instructions are for Claude staying inside it.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics uploads a nightly export from its dispatch system into the dispatch Project. The export's column headers are the vendor's own: `leg_eta_calc`, `svc_ldr_min`, `hold_flag_2`, `drv_hrs_bal`.
questions.stem: Claude summarises the export well in structure but keeps getting values wrong. It reports dwell times in hours when `svc_ldr_min` is in minutes, and it treats `hold_flag_2 = 2` as a yes. Planners have stopped trusting the summaries. What is the MOST appropriate fix?

options.text: Add a short reference document to the Project's knowledge defining each column, its units and its allowed values, and instruct Claude to read it whenever it works with the export.
Ask Claude to state in every summary which units it is assuming for each column, so planners can correct it.
Ask the dispatch systems team to re-export the data every night with renamed, self-explanatory column headers.
Stop using the export and have planners paste the handful of figures they actually need into each chat.

questions.explanation: Units and code meanings are **facts about the source that Claude cannot infer** from column names, so they belong in the Project's knowledge as a small reference document — a data dictionary. Because the export arrives each night with the same headers, that one document keeps working indefinitely, and an instruction ties it to the right situation.

whyWrong.B: This moves the work onto every reader and leaves the numbers wrong. Labelling a wrong unit does not correct it.
whyWrong.C: Plausible and effective once, but it depends on the vendor's systems team re-exporting in a new shape forever, and it changes a system outside the Project's control to solve a documentation problem.
whyWrong.D: Handing the burden back to planners discards the automation that made the Project worthwhile.

questions.mindset: Facts Claude cannot infer — units, code meanings, field definitions — are knowledge, not instructions.

questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy's maintenance planner asks Claude to compare last month's gas usage against budget. The figures sit in a Google Sheet in the company's shared drive, and the Google Workspace connector is enabled on her workspace.
questions.stem: She pastes the question into a new chat and Claude replies that it cannot access company files. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: Connectors only work on documents that have already been uploaded to a Project, not on files that are still in the drive.
Claude can only use files added to the current chat, made available as Project knowledge, or reachable through a source the user has connected to their own account.
Shared drive files are readable by Claude only once the workspace Owner has enabled the connector for the whole organisation.
Once any connector is active, Claude can read every document in the company drive regardless of who is signed in.

questions.explanation: Claude has no ambient access to company systems. Content reaches it in one of three ways: added to the conversation, made available as project knowledge, or reached through a connector **the individual has connected to their own account** — which is why reachability follows that person's file permissions. If a file was never shared with her, no workspace setting will surface it.

whyWrong.A: Connectors exist precisely so live sources don't have to be re-uploaded. Reading a file that lives in the drive is their main purpose.
whyWrong.C: The Owner controls which connectors are *available*, but access to a specific document follows the connected user's own permissions, not an organisation-wide grant.
whyWrong.D: This overstates reachability. Claude sees what the connected account can reach through the connected source, not everything that account could open.

questions.mindset: No ambient access: content must be added, uploaded, or reached through a source the person connected themselves.

questions.scenario: Fernwood Legal's intake team uses a Project to summarise incoming client emails and draft first responses. Each intake clerk connects their own Gmail account.
questions.stem: Since two clerks moved to a shared `intake@fernwood` mailbox, the Project's summaries have started missing client threads and sometimes include a clerk's own personal correspondence. What is the BEST correction?

options.text: Add an instruction naming the shared mailbox and telling Claude to ignore anything to or from a personal account.
Have the two clerks connect the shared `intake@` account instead of their own Gmail accounts, since a connector reads with each person's permissions.
Upload a copy of each client thread to the Project as a file, so the summaries no longer depend on which mailbox is connected.
Restrict the Project to the two clerks and open a second Project for the rest of the intake team.

questions.explanation: A connector reads **as the person who connected it**. If client correspondence now arrives in a shared mailbox, the shared mailbox has to be the connected account — otherwise summaries are built from the wrong stream and personal mail leaks into a shared Project. Fixing it at the connection removes the problem at its source; an instruction can only ask Claude to ignore what it has already been given.

whyWrong.A: Personal mail is still being delivered into the connected mailbox. An instruction cannot un-see it, and it does not change what is read.
whyWrong.C: Manual re-uploading reintroduces exactly the upkeep connectors remove, and the copies fall behind the mailbox within days.
whyWrong.D: Changing who can use the Project does not change which mailbox is being read.

questions.mindset: A connector's view is the connected user's view — fix the connection, don't filter the output.

questions.scenario: Arikon Freight runs Claude Team. Its new compliance officer is completing the module on knowledge sources and connectors and has written down five statements to check with her manager.
questions.stem: Which TWO of the officer's statements about a Team workspace's knowledge and connectors are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Each person connects their own Google Workspace account, so what Claude can reach depends on that person's file permissions.
The workspace Owner can control which connectors are available and which actions they are permitted to take.
Whatever any member uploads or adds becomes visible to everyone who can use that Project.
Once the drive connector is enabled, Claude can read every document in the company drive regardless of who is signed in.
Uploading a file creates a live link, so later edits to the original document are picked up automatically.

questions.explanation: A and B are both accurate, and both matter for governance. **A** explains why reachability is per-person: the connection is made with an individual's account and inherits their permissions. **B** is the control point: the Owner decides which connectors exist and what they may do, which is where governance settings such as allowing only reading and drafting belong.

whyWrong.C: What a Project exposes is governed by that Project's own access settings. A file added to a private Project does not become organisation-wide, and adding something to a shared Project is exactly why sharing needs to be a deliberate decision.
whyWrong.D: This is the most dangerous misconception on the list. Reach follows the connected user's permissions, so one person's connection never exposes the whole drive.
whyWrong.E: An upload is a snapshot taken at upload time. Only content added from its live source stays current — which is why fast-changing material belongs there.

questions.mindset: Knowledge visibility follows Project access; connector reach follows the connected user, and the Owner sets the limits.

questions.scenario: Halberd Insurance keeps its claim-handling policies as scanned PDFs in a shared drive, because the signed originals are scans and no text version exists.
questions.stem: Handlers upload a scanned 40-page policy PDF to the claims Project and ask questions about it. Claude answers fluently, but the clause numbers and dates it cites do not match the document, and handlers have already sent two confidently wrong replies to claimants. Which TWO actions would address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Instruct Claude to quote longer passages from the file when answering, so handlers can check the wording more easily.
Replace the scans with text-based sources — an OCR'd or typed copy, or a link to a live text version.
Keep the scans and add an instruction telling Claude to say when it is unsure instead of answering.
Have handlers verify any specific clause that decides a claim before the reply is sent to the claimant.
Add a second Project containing only the two policies queried most often, so the most important answers become more reliable.

questions.explanation: Claude reads **text, not pixels**. A scan gives it an image and no reliable words, so when asked about a clause it composes something plausible rather than reading it — which means B addresses the cause by giving it text (OCR or a typed copy, or a live text version). D addresses the consequence: for a claim that turns on a specific clause, a human confirms the clause against the actual document before anything reaches a claimant.

whyWrong.A: If the text isn't there, a longer quote is still invented — and a longer fabricated passage looks more authoritative, not less.
whyWrong.C: An uncertainty rule is worth having, but the underlying problem is that the content is unreadable. It lowers confidence without making the document available.
whyWrong.E: Choosing which scans to keep does not make any of them readable, and a second Project doubles the places to maintain.

questions.mindset: If the source isn't machine-readable, no instruction makes it readable — fix the source.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics' dispatch Project draws on the company's price list, which lives in the shared drive and is updated weekly by finance.
questions.stem: The Project's knowledge holds three copies of that price list — a PDF exported in March, a CSV exported in June, and last week's PDF — alongside the live sheet added from the drive. Claude's answers about fuel surcharges vary from chat to chat, and finance cannot tell which copy is being quoted. Which TWO changes resolve this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep the live sheet added from the drive as the single pricing source and delete the stale exports.
Add an instruction that surcharges come only from that current pricing document in the Project's knowledge.
Delete just the March export, on the assumption that Claude prefers the most recently uploaded copy.
Rename each remaining copy with its export date at the front, so it is obvious at a glance which is newest.
Copy the surcharge rules into the Project instructions so they apply regardless of which file is used.

questions.explanation: Three copies of one fact will disagree, and nothing tells Claude which to trust. The durable pattern is **one authoritative source plus a rule that says so**: the live linked sheet stays current because finance maintains it (A), and the instruction closes the door on the old figures (B). Every future change then needs no re-upload at all.

whyWrong.C: There is no rule that picks the newest upload, and two surviving copies can still disagree with each other.
whyWrong.D: Dates help a human reader, not the model. Nothing in the instructions says which copy wins when they conflict.
whyWrong.E: This moves the duplication rather than removing it: the surcharge rules now live in two places that can drift apart again next quarter.

questions.mindset: Duplicated sources of one fact are the bug. Keep one authoritative source and say in the instructions that it wins.

questions.scenario: Riverton City's planning team has built a Project to summarise public consultation responses on a proposed bus route. Only two officers use it, and both are experienced planners.
questions.stem: The Project currently holds the consultation response form and a summary of the 2,400 comments received. What is MISSING from the configuration, and what should it contain?

options.text: Nothing — with only experienced users, the Project works well without instructions.

Project instructions setting the audience (residents, no planning background), the tone, the required structure of a summary, and what to do when a comment raises something the form did not ask about.
A larger model, so the summaries handle 2,400 comments with more nuance.
Connectors to the council's systems, so summaries draw on live case data as well as the comments.

questions.explanation: Instructions are about **how to answer**, and they matter most precisely when the audience is not the people who built the Project. Two officers do not need to say "for residents with no planning background" every time; the Project should. Defining the audience, tone, output structure and the off-form case is what makes the summary consistent and safe to publish.

whyWrong.A: Instructions protect the readers, not the authors. Residents never see the officers' knowledge — they only see the output.
whyWrong.C: A model upgrade changes phrasing quality, not the undefined audience, tone and structure that produce inconsistent output.
whyWrong.D: Connectors would widen the data the Project can see. The gap here is behavioural, and pulling in live case data raises privacy questions nobody has reviewed.

questions.mindset: If the output's readers are not the people who set the Project up, the Project should describe them.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Renewables' project office asks Claude to draft executive updates for live wind-farm projects. The instructions say: "Draft an update for the named project. Keep it to one page."
questions.stem: In practice Claude writes a confident update even when the requester supplies nothing but a project name — it invents turbine availability, output figures and grid constraints. Two updates have gone to the executive committee with figures nobody could source. Which change to the instructions addresses the root cause?

options.text: "Never include a number in an update unless it appears in the project file the requester has attached."
"If the requester has not provided the figures the update needs, ask for them and say which ones are missing before you draft."
"Add a line at the end of every update reading 'Figures pending verification by the project engineer.'"
"Prefer round, presentable figures over decimal precision, since executives prefer clean numbers."

questions.explanation: The failure is that nothing tells Claude what to do when the **request** is incomplete, so it fills the gap. A rule that makes the gap explicit — ask for the specific missing items, name them, don't draft yet — turns a silent guess into a visible question. Grounding rules like A help once material is supplied, but they don't stop the draft being written from nothing.

whyWrong.A: It constrains the content of a draft but still lets Claude write a complete-looking update with no figures at all — or with plausible ones it believes are standard.
whyWrong.C: A disclaimer travels with the numbers. The committee still reads invented figures, now with a note that they may be wrong.
whyWrong.D: This actively encourages the behaviour the team is trying to stop by making tidy numbers the goal.

questions.mindset: When input is missing, instruct Claude to name what it needs — otherwise it will confidently supply it.

questions.scenario: Colleagues at a regional law firm have added rules to their document-drafting Project over two years. It now contains 30 numbered rules, several of them duplicated, two that contradict each other, and one that names a former colleague who has left.
questions.stem: Drafts have become inconsistent and the team cannot tell which rules are live. What is the MOST effective way to restore reliable behaviour?

options.text: Re-number every rule so each has a unique number, and put the most important ones first.
Work out which rules are still true, remove duplicates and the contradiction, and move reference material such as precedent clauses into Project knowledge.
Add a rule at the top saying "follow all 30 rules strictly, and if two conflict, follow the earlier one."
Move all 30 rules into each drafter's account-wide instructions so they apply everywhere, including in chats outside the Project.

questions.explanation: Thirty accumulated lines compete for attention, and reference material sitting among them adds noise rather than rules. The work is editorial: establish which rules are still true, delete duplicates, resolve the contradiction deliberately, and move anything that is **reference content** into knowledge where Claude can consult it when relevant. Fewer, live rules beat more, stale ones.

whyWrong.A: Renumbering and reordering leaves duplicates, contradictions and obsolete references exactly where they were, still competing for attention.
whyWrong.C: A tie-breaker between contradictory rules hides the fact that the instructions are broken, and "follow all 30 strictly" makes the clutter worse.
whyWrong.D: Every rule would then apply in unrelated chats, and each drafter would hold a separate copy — multiplying the drift rather than ending it.

questions.mindset: Short instructions with only live rules beat long ones; reference material belongs in knowledge.

questions.scenario: Calder & Sons is a scaffolding contractor. One Claude Project is used by all four regional offices to draft quotes from site surveys. Each office has added rules over two years: one says never mention scaffold hire costs, another never quote a rate without a site photo, a third never use the word shoring.
questions.stem: Quotes are now blocked in some offices and inconsistent in others, and no one can tell which rule is being applied to a given job. What is the BEST way to fix the instructions?

options.text: Make the three rules the highest priority in the Project instructions, so they are applied consistently everywhere.
Rewrite each rule with the condition it applies to — which region, which job type, why it exists — so each is scoped rather than absolute.
Replace the three rules with a single general instruction to quote professionally and consistently with company policy.
Remove the three rules and add a note in each office's chats reminding staff of the local requirement.

questions.explanation: Unconditional rules get applied to everything, which is why a rule written for one office now blocks quotes in another. Each rule here has a real, narrow reason — a particular region's contract terms, or a safety-dependent cost. Rewriting them with their **condition and their motivation** lets Claude apply the intent to cases nobody listed, which is exactly what the prompting guidance recommends.

whyWrong.A: Raising their prominence makes the over-application more consistent, not less. A blanket ban on hire costs is now enforced in the office that needs them.
whyWrong.C: One vague sentence replaces three specific rules with no content at all. Claude has nothing to follow.
whyWrong.D: The requirements move out of the configuration and into people's memory. They were already being forgotten, which is why they were written down.

questions.mindset: Absolute rules apply absolutely. Scope every rule to a condition and give the reason.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Legal's knowledge-management team maintains Project configurations used by 40 fee-earners. They keep a spreadsheet of every Project with its owner, purpose, last review date and known issues.
questions.stem: The team has found that Project instructions accumulate one-off rules from individual incidents, that superseded policy documents linger in knowledge bases for months, and that nobody removes them. What is the MOST effective structural improvement?

options.text: Add a rule to every Project's instructions saying to ignore any document marked as superseded or archived.
Schedule recurring reviews tied to each policy's actual update cycle, at which the owner removes superseded documents and re-tests with known questions.
Ask each Project owner to review their Project once a year and update it as needed.
Move all policy documents into one shared folder and have every Project reference the folder instead of holding its own copies.

questions.explanation: Maintenance has to be **scheduled against how fast the content actually changes**, or it doesn't happen. A quarterly expense policy will drift within a quarter; a rarely-changing contract template will not. Anchoring the review to the content's real update cycle means superseded documents get removed while they are still recent enough to cause wrong answers, and re-testing with known questions shows whether the Project still behaves.

whyWrong.A: This depends on Claude recognising which documents are superseded — the very judgement that has been failing — and leaves the misleading document in the knowledge base.
whyWrong.C: An annual cycle is longer than the life of many policies, so stale documents are being used for most of a year. It also reviews without testing.
whyWrong.D: One shared folder sounds tidier but creates a single point where unrelated policies mix, and it doesn't assign anyone the job of removing what has been superseded.

questions.mindset: Tie the review to the rate the content changes, and always re-test known answers afterwards.

questions.scenario: Torrington Water's IT team runs a Claude Project for staff password resets and VPN problems. Its instructions say: "Never reveal passwords, PINs, or any part of someone's security question. If a user gives you one, refuse and tell them to contact the service desk directly."
questions.stem: The service desk has noticed users pasting one-time passcodes and security answers straight into the Project chat, which the instructions then refuse to act on. What is the BEST change to how the team handles this?

options.text: Rewrite the rule so Claude may use a code the user supplies in order to help them, but never repeat it back in the reply.
Keep the instruction, and add a notice at the top of the Project telling users not to paste secrets, along with a link to the self-service reset page.
Add an instruction telling Claude to redact anything that looks like a password from its reply, but still use it to help the user.
Remove the rule, on the grounds that refusing to help is frustrating and users will go elsewhere for help anyway.

questions.explanation: The instruction is correct and should stay — it's a genuine security boundary. What's missing is the **upstream control**: users shouldn't be arriving with secrets in the first place. Telling the audience, in the place they see before they type, and giving them a route that doesn't need a secret, addresses the behaviour the instruction is reacting to. The instruction is the backstop, not the fix.

whyWrong.A: This removes a real security control. A passcode pasted into a chat should never be used, even if it isn't echoed back.
whyWrong.C: Redacting the reply leaves the secret in the conversation and still relies on the model to spot it. It weakens the rule without preventing disclosure.
whyWrong.D: Removing the rule creates the risk this instruction exists to prevent. Convenience is not a reason to let a control lapse.

questions.mindset: If an instruction keeps having to block the same bad behaviour, fix what brings users to the Project.

questions.scenario: Fenmoor Group's tax team built one Project per client engagement. Each holds the client's ledgers, uploaded contracts and about 200 chats. A two-year engagement ended this month, and the contract requires all client material to be deleted from company systems.
questions.stem: The Project owner must close the Project down correctly. Which TWO steps are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Confirm with the engagement owner and the firm's privacy contact what has to go and what has to be retained.
Remove the client material from the Project's knowledge and instructions, delete the Project's chats, and record that the deletion was done.
Export the chats to the engagement file, then delete the Project, so the firm's own records stay complete.
Switch the Project to view-only so no new material is added, and leave it in place for reference.
Replace the client name with a code throughout the knowledge and keep the Project for future reference.

questions.explanation: Ending the engagement ends the **purpose** for the data, and the contract requires deletion. Both halves matter: confirm with the people who own the contract and the privacy position rather than deciding alone (A), then remove the material from **knowledge and instructions as well as chats** and record the deletion so it is auditable (B). Knowledge matters as much as chats — stale documents would keep being drawn on.

whyWrong.C: Exporting the material before deleting it copies the data into a second system and defeats the deletion requirement.
whyWrong.D: View-only is still retention. The contract requires the material to be removed, not made read-only.
whyWrong.E: Pseudonymising a client's financial records leaves personal data about a real client in the workspace. It is a redaction, not a deletion.

questions.mindset: When the purpose ends, the data goes with it — and confirm with the owners before deciding.

questions.scenario: Marden & Vale's managing director has used Claude for two years to prepare board papers. His account-wide instructions still say he is the commercial director at a previous employer and ask for "short, punchy executive summaries with lots of buzzwords."
questions.stem: He now needs board papers to be formal, evidence-led and free of hype, and the current settings are quietly shaping them. What should he do?

options.text: Delete all account-wide instructions and rewrite them from scratch describing his current role and the board's expectations.
Review the account-wide instructions line by line, keep the parts that still hold, and replace what no longer applies with his current role and output preferences.
Add a Project for board papers with strong instructions, leaving his account-wide instructions alone because they belong to his personal chats.
Add a single line to his account-wide instructions saying "ignore the buzzwords guidance when writing for the board."

questions.explanation: Personal settings go stale exactly like project settings, and this one is doing real damage: a demand for buzzwords pulls against formal, evidence-led board papers in **every** conversation. Reviewing line by line is the right move — it keeps the preferences that still help him, removes the ones that now misdescribe his role, and updates output preferences to the ones he actually wants. Two years of accumulated settings deserve an audit, not a nuclear clear.

whyWrong.A: Throwing away everything discards years of useful preferences he would have to rebuild from nothing, including ones that are still correct.
whyWrong.C: A Project instruction competes with the account-wide rule instead of removing it, and the conflict would surface in ordinary chats too.
whyWrong.D: This adds a contradicting rule rather than removing the harmful one, leaving two instructions pulling in opposite directions.

questions.mindset: Account-wide settings drift too. Audit them line by line rather than deleting or patching.

questions.scenario: Ivybridge College's admissions team uses a Claude Project to answer applicant questions, holding the current course prospectus, the entry requirements, and an FAQ. About 60 staff and several current students can use it.
questions.stem: The prospectus is updated every September. Last September a colleague uploaded the new version but forgot to delete the old one, and since then the Project has given contradictory entry requirements about a third of the time. Students have complained, and staff no longer know which document is correct. Which TWO actions would BEST fix this and keep it fixed? Choose TWO.

options.text: Delete the superseded prospectus and, going forward, keep only the current version in the Project's knowledge — one source per fact.
Add an instruction telling Claude always to use the most recently dated prospectus when two versions are present.
Run a short set of known-answer questions now to confirm the Project gives the current requirements, and keep them to re-test after each future update.
Ask admissions staff to report any answer that looks like it came from the old document, and correct those cases as they arrive.
Give every member of the admissions team edit access so that whoever spots an old document can replace it immediately.

questions.explanation: Two failures need two fixes. The **immediate** one is that two copies of the same fact are live, and no tie-breaker makes that reliable — the outdated document has to go. The **preventative** one is a repeatable test: a handful of known-answer questions confirms the Project is right now and, re-run after each September update, catches the same mistake before students do.

whyWrong.A: This papers over the duplicate instead of removing it. The stale text remains in the knowledge base, and "most recently dated" is a rule Claude may apply inconsistently.
whyWrong.D: Waiting for complaints means students get wrong answers first. Reactive correction fixes individual cases, not the configuration that caused them.
whyWrong.E: Spreading edit rights is how the superseded document got uploaded in the first place. Someone needs to own the knowledge base for a recurring update like this.

questions.mindset: Remove the duplicate, then keep a known-answer test so the next update can't fail the same way.
